question: Under paragraph 4.2.2(ii) of the Master Circular, what minimum Common Equity Tier 1 capital ratio must a bank maintain on an ongoing basis?
options: 2.5% of risk-weighted assets
7.0% of risk-weighted assets
9.0% of risk-weighted assets
5.5% of risk-weighted assets
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.2(ii)
source_excerpt: Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital must be at least 5.5% of risk-weighted assets (RWAs) i.e., for credit risk + market risk + operational risk on an ongoing basis.

question: What does paragraph 4.2.2(iii) set as the minimum Tier 1 capital ratio, and what maximum Additional Tier 1 capital does it allow within that ratio?
options: 6.5% of RWAs with Additional Tier 1 capped at 2.0%
8.0% of RWAs with Additional Tier 1 capped at 1.5%
9.0% of RWAs with Additional Tier 1 capped at 2.0%
7% of RWAs with Additional Tier 1 capped at 1.5%
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.2(iii)
source_excerpt: Tier 1 capital must be at least 7% of RWAs on an ongoing basis. Thus, within the minimum Tier 1 capital, Additional Tier 1 capital can be admitted maximum at 1.5% of RWAs.

question: According to paragraph 4.2.2(iv), what minimum total capital must a bank hold, and how much Tier 2 capital may be admitted within it?
options: 11.5% of RWAs with Tier 2 admitted up to 2.5%
8.0% of RWAs with Tier 2 admitted up to 1.5%
9% of RWAs with Tier 2 admitted up to 2%
10% of RWAs with Tier 2 admitted up to 1.5%
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.2(iv)
source_excerpt: Total Capital (Tier 1 Capital plus Tier 2 Capital) must be at least 9% of RWAs on an ongoing basis. Thus, within the minimum CRAR of 9%, Tier 2 capital can be admitted maximum up to 2%.

question: What does paragraph 15.2.1 require every bank to maintain above the regulatory minimum capital requirement, and of what form is it?
options: A capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, comprised of Common Equity Tier 1 capital
A capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, comprised of Additional Tier 1 capital
A countercyclical capital buffer of 1.5%, comprised of Tier 2 capital
A capital conservation buffer of 4.0%, comprised of Common Equity Tier 1 capital
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 15.2.1
source_excerpt: Banks are required to maintain a capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, comprised of Common Equity Tier 1 capital, above the regulatory minimum capital requirement

question: How does paragraph 4.1 state the minimum Pillar 1 Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio, and how does it treat the capital buffers?
options: 9% on an on-going basis, other than capital conservation buffer and countercyclical capital buffer
9% on an on-going basis including both the capital conservation and countercyclical buffers
11.5% on an on-going basis including the capital conservation buffer
8% on an on-going basis excluding every capital buffer
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.1
source_excerpt: Banks shall maintain a minimum Pillar 1 Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 9% on an on-going basis (other than capital conservation buffer and countercyclical capital buffer etc.).

question: How does the footnote to paragraph 4.2.1 distinguish going-concern capital from gone-concern capital?
options: Going-concern capital absorbs losses only in a situation of liquidation, while gone-concern capital absorbs losses without triggering bankruptcy
Both going-concern and gone-concern capital absorb losses only when the bank is liquidated
Going-concern capital absorbs losses without triggering bankruptcy; gone-concern capital absorbs losses only in liquidation
Gone-concern capital is the capital that absorbs losses in the normal course of business
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.1, footnote 5
source_excerpt: From regulatory capital perspective, going-concern capital is the capital which can absorb losses without triggering bankruptcy of the bank. Gone-concern capital is the capital which will absorb losses only in a situation of liquidation of the bank.

question: Under paragraph 4.4.1, from which component of capital must goodwill and all other intangible assets be deducted?
options: From Tier 2 capital only, to the extent it exceeds 2% of RWAs
From Additional Tier 1 capital, at the discretion of the bank
From Tier 1 capital, but only the amount above 10% of capital funds
From Common Equity Tier 1 capital
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.4.1(i)
source_excerpt: Goodwill and all other intangible assets should be deducted from Common Equity Tier 1 capital including any goodwill included in the valuation of significant investments in the capital of banking, financial and insurance entities which are outside the scope of regulatory consolidation.

question: What minimum leverage ratio does paragraph 16.2.2 prescribe for domestic systemically important banks and for other banks respectively?
options: 5% for D-SIBs and 4% for other banks
3% for D-SIBs and 2.5% for other banks
4% for every bank irrespective of systemic importance
4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other banks
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 16.2.2
source_excerpt: The minimum Leverage Ratio shall be 4% for Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) and 3.5% for other banks

question: How does paragraph 16.2.1 define the Basel III leverage ratio?
options: Common Equity Tier 1 capital divided by total risk-weighted assets, expressed as a percentage
Tier 2 capital divided by the exposure measure, expressed as a decimal fraction
The capital measure divided by the exposure measure, expressed as a percentage
Tier 1 capital divided by the capital conservation buffer, expressed as a percentage
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 16.2.1
source_excerpt: The Basel III leverage ratio is defined as the capital measure (the numerator) divided by the exposure measure (the denominator), with this ratio expressed as a percentage.

question: Which capital measure does paragraph 16.3 specify as the numerator to be used for the leverage ratio?
options: Common Equity Tier 1 capital of the risk-based capital framework
Total capital comprising Tier 1 and Tier 2 of the risk-based framework
Additional Tier 1 capital of the risk-based capital framework
Tier 1 capital of the risk-based capital framework
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 16.3
source_excerpt: The capital measure for the leverage ratio is the Tier 1 capital of the risk-based capital framework

question: According to paragraph 16.4.1, which four groups of exposures together make up a bank's total leverage ratio exposure measure?
options: On-balance sheet exposures and derivative exposures only, with securities financing transactions excluded
On-balance sheet exposures, derivative exposures, SFT exposures and off-balance sheet items
Credit risk, market risk, operational risk and counterparty credit risk exposures
Only the on-balance sheet non-derivative exposures recorded at accounting value
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 16.4.1(iii)
source_excerpt: A bank's total exposure measure is the sum of the following exposures: (a) on-balance sheet exposures; (b) derivative exposures; (c) securities financing transaction (SFT) exposures; and (d) off-balance sheet (OBS) items.

question: Under paragraph 3.1(a), which entities are excluded when capital adequacy is measured at the consolidated (Group) level?
options: Those engaged in insurance and any non-financial activities
Subsidiaries engaged in banking and financial services
Joint ventures and associates incorporated outside India
Wholly owned subsidiaries of foreign banks operating in India
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 3.1(a)
source_excerpt: capital adequacy ratio requirements, which measure the capital adequacy of a bank based on its capital strength and risk profile after consolidating the assets and liabilities of its subsidiaries / joint ventures / associates etc. except those engaged in insurance and any non-financial activities

question: What does paragraph 3.4.1 direct about the consolidation of subsidiaries for the purpose of capital adequacy?
options: Only insurance subsidiaries should be consolidated for capital adequacy
No subsidiary should be consolidated; only solo level capital adequacy applies
All banking and other financial subsidiaries except insurance and non-financial ones should be fully consolidated
Every subsidiary of the bank, including those engaged in insurance and non-financial activities, should be fully consolidated
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 3.4.1
source_excerpt: All banking and other financial subsidiaries except subsidiaries engaged in insurance and any non-financial activities (both regulated and unregulated) should be fully consolidated for the purpose of capital adequacy

question: How does paragraph 3.4.2 treat the equity and other regulatory capital investments in insurance and non-financial subsidiaries?
options: They are added to the Common Equity Tier 1 capital of the consolidated banking group
They are risk-weighted at 100% in the consolidated capital adequacy framework
They are deducted from consolidated regulatory capital of the group
They are recognised as Additional Tier 1 capital of the parent bank
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 3.4.2
source_excerpt: The equity and other regulatory capital investments in the insurance and non-financial subsidiaries will be deducted from consolidated regulatory capital of the group.

question: According to paragraph 3.5.1, what must be done at solo level with investments in the capital instruments of subsidiaries that are consolidated in the group's financial statements?
options: They shall be deducted from the corresponding capital instruments issued by the bank
They shall be added to the Common Equity Tier 1 capital of the bank
They shall be deducted only from the capital conservation buffer
They need not be deducted at solo level because the group already consolidates those subsidiaries
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 3.5.1
source_excerpt: In addition, investments in the capital instruments of the subsidiaries, which are consolidated in the consolidated financial statements of the group, shall be deducted from the corresponding capital instruments issued by the bank.

question: What minimum capital adequacy ratio does paragraph 3.3 require a foreign bank's Wholly Owned Subsidiary to maintain for an initial period after it commences operations?
options: 8 per cent on a continuous basis for an initial period of five years from the date of commencement of its operations
10 per cent on a continuous basis for an initial period of three years from the commencement of its operations
12 per cent on an ongoing basis for the first year and 10 per cent thereafter
9 per cent for an initial period of two years from the commencement of its operations
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 3.3
source_excerpt: WOS shall, however, maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio, on a continuous basis for an initial period of three years from the commencement of its operations, at 10 per cent.

question: Under paragraph 4.2.3.1, at what discount may revaluation reserves arising on revaluation of a bank's property be reckoned as Common Equity Tier 1 capital?
options: At a discount of 45 per cent, subject to conditions
At a discount of 25 per cent, subject to conditions
At a discount of 10 per cent, subject to conditions
At a discount of 55 per cent, subject to conditions
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.3.1.A(vi)
source_excerpt: Revaluation reserves arising out of change in the carrying amount of a bank's property consequent upon its revaluation may be reckoned as CET1 capital at a discount of 55 per cent, subject to meeting the following conditions

question: Which of the following is listed in paragraph 4.2.4.1 as an element of Additional Tier 1 capital for Indian banks?
options: Debt capital instruments complying with the requirements of Annex 5
Preference share capital instruments complying with the requirements of Annex 6
General provisions and loss reserves held against future unidentified losses
Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares (PNCPS) complying with Annex 3
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.4.1.A(i)
source_excerpt: Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares (PNCPS), which comply with the regulatory requirements as specified in Annex 3

question: Under paragraph 4.2.5.1, up to what maximum amount are general provisions and loss reserves admitted as Tier 2 capital under the standardized approach?
options: 0.6% of credit risk weighted assets, the limit that applies under the Internal Ratings Based approach
2.0% of total risk weighted assets under the standardized approach
1.25% of the total credit risk weighted assets under the standardized approach
1.5% of credit risk weighted assets under the standardized approach
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.5.1.A(i)
source_excerpt: However, these items together will be admitted as Tier 2 capital up to a maximum of 1.25% of the total credit risk weighted assets under the standardized approach

question: What does paragraph 4.2.5.1 provide about the Investment Fluctuation Reserve and its inclusion in regulatory capital?
options: It qualifies for Tier 2 capital only up to 1.25% of credit risk weighted assets
It qualifies for inclusion in Tier 2 capital without any ceiling
It must be deducted from Common Equity Tier 1 capital in full
It qualifies only for inclusion in Additional Tier 1 capital
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.5.1.A(i)(b)
source_excerpt: Investment Fluctuation Reserve shall also qualify for inclusion in Tier 2 capital, without any ceiling

question: Which of the following is listed in paragraph 4.2.3.1 as an element of Common Equity Tier 1 capital for Indian banks?
options: Head Office borrowings in foreign currency kept in separate Indian books
General provisions held against future, presently unidentified losses
Perpetual Debt Instruments complying with the requirements of Annex 4
Statutory reserves
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.2.3.1.A
source_excerpt: Common shares (paid-up equity capital) issued by the bank which meet the criteria for classification as common shares for regulatory purposes as given in Annex 1; (ii) Stock surplus (share premium) resulting from the issue of common shares; (iii) Statutory reserves;

question: How does paragraph 4.4.2(i) require deferred tax assets associated with accumulated losses and similar assets to be treated?
options: They shall be deducted in full from CET1 capital
They may be recognised in CET1 capital up to 10% of CET1 capital
They shall be deducted from Tier 2 capital of the bank
They shall be risk-weighted at 250% and retained in Tier 1
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.4.2(i)
source_excerpt: Deferred tax assets (DTAs) associated with accumulated losses and other such assets shall be deducted in full, from CET1 capital.

question: What does paragraph 4.4.2(ii) permit for deferred tax assets that relate to timing differences rather than accumulated losses?
options: They must be deducted in full from CET1 capital under all circumstances without any exception
They may be recognised in CET1 capital up to 15% of a bank's CET1 capital at the discretion of banks
They may be recognised in CET1 capital up to 10% of a bank's CET1 capital, at the discretion of banks
They may be recognised in Tier 2 capital up to 10% of Tier 2 capital
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.4.2(ii)
source_excerpt: DTAs which relate to timing differences (other than those related to accumulated losses) may, instead of full deduction from CET1 capital, be recognised in the CET1 capital up to 10% of a bank's CET1 capital, at the discretion of banks

question: How does paragraph 4.4.8(i) treat a bank's investment in its own shares?
options: It is tantamount to repayment of capital and must be knocked off from the bank's capital
It may be included in Additional Tier 1 capital at the discretion of the bank
It counts as Common Equity Tier 1 capital if held for more than five working days
It is deducted from Tier 2 capital only, and only when the bank holds it through mutual funds or index funds
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.4.8(i)
source_excerpt: Investment in a bank's own shares is tantamount to repayment of capital and therefore, it is necessary to knock-off such investment from the bank's capital with a view to improving the bank's quality of capital

question: Under paragraph 4.4.9.2(A), how are reciprocal cross holdings of capital in banking, financial and insurance entities treated?
options: They are recognised in Tier 1 capital up to 10% of the bank's capital funds
They are risk-weighted at 100% when held in the banking book
Such holdings of capital will be fully deducted
They are deducted only from Tier 2 capital of the investee entity
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, paragraph 4.4.9.2(A)
source_excerpt: Reciprocal cross holdings of capital might result in artificially inflating the capital position of banks. Such holdings of capital will be fully deducted.

question: Under the Standardised Approach, what risk weight applies to both fund-based and non-fund based claims on the central government?
options: 20 per cent
50 per cent
Zero risk weight
100 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.2.1
source_excerpt: Both fund based and non-fund based claims on the central government will attract a zero risk weight. Central Government guaranteed claims will attract a zero risk weight.

question: What risk weight do claims guaranteed by a State Government attract under the Standardised Approach?
options: 20 per cent
Zero risk weight
50 per cent
100 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.2.2
source_excerpt: The Direct loan / credit / overdraft exposure, if any, of banks to the State Governments and the investment in State Government securities will attract zero risk weight. State Government guaranteed claims will attract 20 per cent risk weight.

question: As per Table 1 of the circular, what risk weight applies to claims on a foreign sovereign rated BBB by S&P/Fitch?
options: 20 per cent
50 per cent
100 per cent
150 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.3, Table 1
source_excerpt: S&P*/Fitch ratings AAA to AA A BBB BB to B Below B Unrated Moody’s ratings Aaa to Aa A Baa Ba to B Below B Unrated Risk weight (%) 0 20 50 100 150 100

question: How does the circular prescribe that claims on domestic public sector entities be risk weighted?
options: In a manner similar to the claims on sovereigns and central governments
In a manner similar to claims on corporates
With a uniform risk weight of 20 per cent
In a manner similar to the claims on banks
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.4.1
source_excerpt: Claims on domestic public sector entities will be risk weighted in a manner similar to claims on Corporates.

topic: risk weights - MDBs, BIS and IMF
question: What risk weight do claims on the BIS, the IMF and the eligible Multilateral Development Banks evaluated by the BCBS attract?
options: A uniform zero per cent risk weight
A uniform twenty per cent risk weight
A uniform fifty per cent risk weight
Risk weights as per the ratings assigned to them
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.5
source_excerpt: Claims on the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the following eligible Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) evaluated by the BCBS will be treated similar to claims on scheduled banks meeting the minimum capital adequacy requirements and assigned a uniform twenty per cent risk weight

question: Claims on a bank denominated in 'domestic' foreign currency and met out of resources in the same currency raised in that jurisdiction attract which risk weight when the bank complies with the minimum CRAR prescribed by its regulator?
options: Zero per cent
Ten per cent
20 per cent
50 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.6.3
source_excerpt: However, the claims on a bank which are denominated in 'domestic 35' foreign currency met out of the resources in the same currency raised in that jurisdiction will be risk weighted at 20 per cent provided the bank complies with the minimum CRAR prescribed by the concerned bank regulator(s).

question: Under Table 5 Part A, what risk weight applies to a long-term claim on a corporate assigned an AA rating by a domestic rating agency?
options: 30 per cent
20 per cent
50 per cent
100 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.8, Table 5
source_excerpt: Domestic rating agencies AAA AA A BBB BB & below Unrated Risk weight (%) 20 30 50 100 150 100

question: What risk weight is assigned to claims included in a regulatory retail portfolio, except as provided for non-performing assets?
options: 75 per cent
50 per cent
100 per cent
125 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.9.1
source_excerpt: Claims (including both fund-based and non-fund based) that meet all the four criteria listed below in paragraph 5.9.3 may be considered as retail claims for regulatory capital purposes and included in a regulatory retail portfolio. Claims included in this portfolio shall be assigned a risk - weight of 75 per cent, except as provided in paragraph 5.12 below for non-performing assets.

question: For claims secured by residential property that fall outside the categories in Table 7, what risk weight does the circular prescribe?
options: A uniform risk weight of 35 per cent irrespective of the purpose of finance
The higher of the risk weight applicable to the counterparty or to the purpose for which the bank has extended finance
The lower of the counterparty risk weight and 75 per cent
A risk weight of 100 per cent irrespective of the counterparty
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.10.2
source_excerpt: All other claims secured by residential property would attract the higher of the risk weight applicable to the counterparty or to the purpose for which the bank has extended finance.

question: What risk weight do claims classified as commercial real estate exposure attract?
options: 100 per cent
75 per cent
125 per cent
150 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.11
source_excerpt: Commercial Real Estate exposure is defined as per the guidelines issued vide circular DBOD.No.BP.BC.42/08.12.015/2009-10 dated September 9, 2009. 5.11.2 Claims mentioned above will attract a risk weight of 100 per cent.

question: Under the risk-weighting framework for non-performing assets, what risk weight applies to the unsecured portion of an NPA when specific provisions are at least 50 per cent of the outstanding amount?
options: 150 per cent
100 per cent
50 per cent
75 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.12.1
source_excerpt: (iii) 50 per cent risk weight when specific provisions are at least 50 per cent of the outstanding amount of the NPA

question: When defining the secured portion of an NPA for capital adequacy purposes, which collateral is recognised?
options: Collateral recognised for credit risk mitigation purposes under paragraph 7.3.5
Land and building valued by an expert valuer with a valuation not more than three years old
Plant and machinery in good working condition at a value not higher than the depreciated value
Current assets of the borrower irrespective of their realisable value
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.12.3
source_excerpt: For the purpose of defining the secured portion of the NPA, eligible collateral will be the same as recognised for credit risk mitigation purposes (paragraph 7.3.5).

question: What risk weight does the circular prescribe for consumer credit exposure, including personal loans, that excludes housing loans, education loans, vehicle loans and loans secured by gold and gold jewellery?
options: 100 per cent
150 per cent
125 per cent
75 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.13.3
source_excerpt: Consumer credit exposure (outstanding as well as new), including personal loans, but excluding housing loans, education loans, vehicle loans and loans secured by gold and gold jewellery, will attract a risk weight of 125 per cent47.

question: What credit conversion factor does Table 8 assign to direct credit substitutes such as general guarantees of indebtedness and acceptances?
options: 50 per cent
100 per cent
20 per cent
0 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.15.2, Table 8
source_excerpt: 1. Direct credit substitutes e.g., general guarantees of indebtedness (including standby L/Cs serving as financial guarantees for loans and securities, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities for securitisation transactions), and acceptances (including endorsements with the character of acceptance). (i.e., the risk of loss depends on the credit worthiness of the counterparty or the party against whom a potential claim is acquired) 100

question: An irrevocable commitment with an original maturity of 15 months to issue a six-month documentary letter of credit attracts which credit conversion factor?
options: 50 per cent
20 per cent
100 per cent
0 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 5.15.2
source_excerpt: Irrevocable commitments to provide off-balance sheet facilities should be assigned the lower of the two applicable credit conversion factors. For example, an irrevocable commitment with an original maturity of 15 months (50 per cent - CCF) to issue a six month documentary letter of credit (20 per cent - CCF) would attract the lower of the CCF i.e., the CCF applicable to the documentary letter of credit viz. 20 per cent.

question: Which of the following is eligible financial collateral under the comprehensive approach?
options: Re-securitisations, irrespective of any credit ratings
Gold, including both bullion and jewellery
Land and building that are valued by an expert valuer
Units of mutual funds where no price for the units is publicly quoted daily
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.3.5
source_excerpt: Gold: Gold would include both bullion and jewellery. However, the value of the collateralised jewellery should be arrived at after notionally converting these to 99.99 purity.

question: Which international credit rating agencies may banks use for risk weighting their claims where specified?
options: Fitch, SEBI and CRISIL Ratings Limited
Moody's, ICRA Limited and CARE Ratings Limited
Fitch, Moody's and Standard & Poor's
Acuite Ratings & Research Limited, Brickwork Ratings India Private Limited and INFOMERICS Valuation and Rating Ltd.
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 6.1.3
source_excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has decided that banks may use the ratings of the following international credit rating agencies (arranged in alphabetical order) for the purposes of risk weighting their claims for capital adequacy purposes where specified: a. Fitch; b. Moody's; and c. Standard & Poor’s

question: Which of the following lists only domestic credit rating agencies whose ratings banks may use for risk weighting their claims?
options: Fitch, Moody's and Standard & Poor's
CRISIL Ratings Limited, ICRA Limited and the Securities and Exchange Board of India
Acuite Ratings & Research Limited, CARE Ratings Limited and Moody's

Acuite Ratings & Research Limited, Brickwork Ratings India Private Limited, CARE Ratings Limited, CRISIL Ratings Limited, ICRA Limited, India Ratings and Research Private Limited and INFOMERICS Valuation and Rating Ltd.
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 6.1.2
source_excerpt: (a) Acuite Ratings & Research Limited (Acuite)78 (b) Brickwork Ratings India Private Limited79 (c) CARE Ratings Limited; (d) CRISIL Ratings Limited80; (e) ICRA Limited; (f) India Ratings and Research Private Limited (India Ratings); and (g) INFOMERICS Valuation and Rating Ltd. (INFOMERICS)81

question: Under the mapping of long-term ratings of the chosen domestic rating agencies, what risk weight is assigned to a rating of A+ or A-?
options: 50 per cent
30 per cent
20 per cent
100 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 6.4.2
source_excerpt: For example, A+ or A - would be considered to be in the A rating category and assigned 50 per cent risk weight.

question: If a short-term rated facility to a counterparty attracts a 50 per cent risk weight, what is the lowest risk weight that unrated short-term claims to the same counterparty may attract?
options: 50 per cent
20 per cent
30 per cent
100 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 6.5.2
source_excerpt: If a short-term rated facility to counterparty attracts a 20 per cent or a 50 per cent risk-weight, unrated short-term claims to the same counter- party cannot attract a risk weight lower than 30 per cent or 100 per cent respectively.

question: Which of the following is a general principle governing the use of credit risk mitigation techniques?
options: The effects of credit risk mitigation may be double counted where an issue-specific rating is used
A transaction using credit risk mitigation techniques should receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction where such techniques are not used
No transaction in which credit risk mitigation techniques are used should receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction where such techniques are not used
Principal-only ratings are allowed within the credit risk mitigation framework
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.1.2
source_excerpt: No transaction in which Credit Risk Mitigation (CRM) techniques are used should receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction where such techniques are not used.

question: What minimum legal documentation standard must be satisfied for a bank to obtain capital relief for credit risk mitigation?
options: Documentation must be notarised in each district where the bank has branches
All documentation used in collateralised transactions and guarantees must be binding on all parties and legally enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions
Documentation need only be enforceable in the jurisdiction where the counterparty is incorporated
Legal review is optional where the collateral consists of cash
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.2
source_excerpt: All documentation used in collateralised transactions and guarantees must be binding on all parties and legally enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions.

question: Which approach to collateralised transactions shall banks in India adopt for credit risk mitigation?
options: The simple approach, which substitutes the risk weighting of the collateral for the risk weighting of the counterparty for the collateralised portion
The standardised approach for market risk
The basic indicator approach for operational risk
The comprehensive approach, which allows fuller offset of collateral against exposures by effectively reducing the exposure amount by the value ascribed to the collateral
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.3.2
source_excerpt: Banks in India shall adopt the Comprehensive Approach, which allows fuller offset of collateral against exposures, by effectively reducing the exposure amount by the value ascribed to the collateral.

question: What standard supervisory haircut applies where the exposure and the collateral are denominated in different currencies?
options: 4 per cent
15 per cent
8 per cent
25 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.3.7
source_excerpt: The standard supervisory haircut for currency risk where exposure and collateral are denominated in different currencies is eight per cent (also based on a 10-business day holding period and daily mark-to-market).

question: Under the substitution approach for guarantees, how does credit protection reduce the capital requirement?
options: The whole exposure is assigned the risk weight of the guarantor irrespective of the amount covered
The risk weight of the counterparty is reduced by the guarantee coverage percentage
Capital charges are reduced even when the guarantor has a higher risk weight than the counterparty
The protected portion of the counterparty exposure is assigned the risk weight of the guarantor, whereas the uncovered portion retains the risk weight of the underlying counterparty
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 7.5.2
source_excerpt: A range of guarantors are recognised and a substitution approach will be applied. Thus , only guarantees issued by entities with a lower risk weight than the counterparty will lead to reduced capital charges since the protected portion of the counterparty exposure is assigned the risk weight of the guarantor, whereas the uncovered portion retains the risk weight of the underlying counterparty.

question: Under section 8.1, which positions are subject to the market risk capital charge?
options: Interest rate related instruments and equities held in the banking book only
Interest rate and equity positions in the trading book, plus foreign exchange risk throughout the bank
Every on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet position irrespective of the book in which it is held
Foreign exchange risk in the trading book only, with interest rate and equity risk confined to the banking book
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.1
source_excerpt: Market risk is defined as the risk of losses in on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet positions arising from movements in market prices. The market risk positions subject to capital charge requirement are: (i) The risks pertaining to interest rate related instruments and equities in the trading book; and (ii) Foreign exchange risk (including open position in precious metals) throughout the bank (both banking and trading books).

question: In which books does section 8.2.1 require capital charges for foreign exchange risk, including gold and other precious metals, to be computed?
options: In the trading book only
In both the trading book and the banking book
In the banking book only
In the trading book for gold and in the banking book for other precious metals
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.2.1
source_excerpt: These guidelines seek to address the issues involved in computing capital charges for interest rate related instruments in the trading book, equities in the trading book and foreign exchange risk (including gold and other precious metals) in both trading and banking books.

question: How does paragraph 8.2.4 convert the market risk capital charge into risk-weighted assets?
options: By multiplying the capital charge by 8
By multiplying the capital charge by 12.5
By dividing the capital charge by 12.5
By multiplying the capital charge by 100 to reflect a full risk weighting
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.2.4
source_excerpt: The risk-weighted assets for market risk should be determined by multiplying the market risk capital charge by a factor of 12.5, as provided in paragraph 8.7.

question: How does section 8.3.3 express the minimum capital requirement for interest rate related instruments?
options: As two separately calculated charges, a specific risk charge and a general market risk charge
As a single charge that merges specific and general market risk
As three separate charges covering default risk, migration risk and volatility risk in the portfolio
As one general market risk charge applied to the whole banking book
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.3.3
source_excerpt: The minimum capital requirement is expressed in terms of two separately calculated charges, (i) "specific risk" charge for each security, which is designed to protect against an adverse movement in the price of an individual security owing to factors related to the individual issuer, both for short (short position is not allowed in India except in derivatives and Central Government Securities) and long positions, and (ii) "general market risk" charge towards interest rate risk in the portfolio

question: Which method has the circular decided banks should adopt to arrive at the capital charge for interest rate risk?
options: Maturity method
Internal risk management models method
Standardised duration method
Standardised maturity method
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.3.8
source_excerpt: Under the standardised method there are two principal methods of measuring market risk, a "maturity" method and a "duration" method. As "duration" method is a more accurate method of measuring interest rate risk, it has been decided to adopt standardised duration method to arrive at the capital charge.

question: Under paragraph 8.4.2, what general market risk charge applies to a bank's gross equity positions?
options: 11.25 per cent
9 per cent
13.5 per cent
12.5 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.4.2
source_excerpt: Capital charge for specific risk (akin to credit risk) will be 11.25 per cent or capital charge in accordance with the risk warranted by external rating (or lack of it) of the counterparty, whichever is higher and specific risk is computed on banks' gross equity positions (i.e., the sum of all long equity positions and of all short equity positions - short equity position is, however, not allowed for banks in India). In addition, the general market risk charge will also be 9 per cent on the gross equity positions.

question: Which item is included when a bank calculates its net open position in a currency under section 8.5?
options: The principal on currency swaps already included in the spot position
A profit or loss denominated in the bank's home currency
The net forward position, being amounts to be received less amounts to be paid under forward foreign exchange transactions
Only guarantees that are certain to be called and likely to be irrecoverable, with the net spot and net forward positions excluded from the calculation
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.5
source_excerpt: The net forward position (i.e., all amounts to be received less all amounts to be paid under forward foreign exchange transactions, including currency futures and the principal on currency swaps not included in the spot position);

question: What capital charge for market risk applies to foreign exchange and gold open positions under section 8.5?
options: 11.25 per cent
12.5 per cent
13.5 per cent
9 per cent
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.5
source_excerpt: Foreign exchange open positions and gold open positions are at present risk-weighted at 100 per cent. Thus, capital charge for market risks in foreign exchange and gold open position is 9 per cent.

question: According to section 8.7, how are the capital charges for specific risk and general market risk treated before aggregation?
options: They are computed separately before aggregation
They are merged into one combined charge before aggregation
The specific risk charge is deducted from the general market risk charge
They are aggregated only for positions in the trading book
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 8.7
source_excerpt: As explained earlier capital charges for specific risk and general market risk are to be computed separately before aggregation. For computing the total capital charge and Risk Weighted Assets for market risks, the calculations may be plotted in the following table:

question: How does section 9.1 define operational risk?
options: The risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, with legal risk excluded
The risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events, including legal risk but excluding strategic and reputational risk
The risk of loss arising only from external events such as natural calamities
The risk of loss that includes strategic risk but excludes legal risk
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 9.1
source_excerpt: Operational risk is defined as the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events. This definition includes legal risk, but excludes strategic and reputational risk.

question: Which three methods for calculating operational risk capital charges are listed in paragraph 9.2.1?
options: Basic Indicator Approach, Internal Ratings Based Approach and Advanced Measurement Approaches
Standardised Approach, Maturity Method and Advanced Measurement Approaches
Basic Indicator Approach, Standardised Approach and Internal Models Method
Basic Indicator Approach, Standardised Approach and Advanced Measurement Approaches
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 9.2.1
source_excerpt: The New Capital Adequacy Framework outlines three methods for calculating operational risk capital charges in a continuum of increasing sophistication and risk sensitivity: (i) the Basic Indicator Approach (BIA); (ii) the Standardised Approach (TSA); and (iii) Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).

question: Which approach do banks in India use to compute operational risk capital requirements under paragraph 9.2.2?
options: The Standardised Approach
The Advanced Measurement Approach
An internal models approach approved by the bank's board
The Basic Indicator Approach
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 9.2.2
source_excerpt: Banks in India shall compute the capital requirements for operational risk under the Basic Indicator Approach. Reserve Bank will review the capital requirement produced by the Basic Indicator Approach for general credibility, especially in relation to a bank's peers and in the event that credibility is lacking, appropriate supervisory action under Pillar 2 will be considered.

question: How does paragraph 9.3.1 state that capital for operational risk is determined under the Basic Indicator Approach?
options: The average over the previous three years of a fixed percentage of positive annual gross income
The average over the previous five years of a fixed percentage of the bank's total assets after deductions
A fixed percentage of the bank's total risk-weighted assets
The largest single-year operational loss recorded in the previous three years
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 9.3.1
source_excerpt: Under the Basic Indicator Approach, banks shall hold capital for operational risk equal to the average over the previous three years of a fixed percentage (denoted as alpha) of positive annual gross income.

question: How is gross income defined for the Basic Indicator Approach in paragraph 9.3.2?
options: Net interest income plus net fee and commission income
Total income before tax as reported in the profit and loss account
Net interest income less operating expenses
Net interest income plus net non-interest income
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 9.3.2
source_excerpt: Gross income is defined as "Net interest income" plus "net non-interest income". It is intended that this measure should: (i) be gross of any provisions (e.g., for unpaid interest) and write-offs made during the year;

question: According to paragraph 9.3.5, how is the operational risk capital charge converted into risk-weighted assets?
options: It is divided by 12.5
It is multiplied by 100 to reflect a full risk weighting
It is multiplied by 12.5
It is multiplied by 8
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 9.3.5
source_excerpt: Once the bank has calculated the capital charge for operational risk under the Basic Indicator Approach, it has to multiply this with 12.5 and arrive at the notional risk weighted asset (RWA) for operational risk.

question: What objective of the Supervisory Review Process is stated in paragraph 10.3?
options: To ensure that banks have adequate capital to support all the risks in their business and to encourage them to develop and use better risk management techniques
To prescribe a single maximum leverage ratio for every bank
To take over the internal capital adequacy assessment process from banks
To set the minimum capital ratio for credit risk only
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 10.3
source_excerpt: The objective of the SRP is to ensure that banks have adequate capital to support all the risks in their business as also to encourage them to develop and use better risk management techniques for monitoring and managing their risks.

topic: ICAAP - risks not captured under Pillar 1
question: Which risk does paragraph 10.4 list as one that is not captured or not fully captured in the regulatory CRAR?
options: Counterparty credit risk on over-the-counter derivatives
Interest rate risk in the banking book
Operational risk measured under the Basic Indicator Approach
Foreign exchange risk in the trading book
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 10.4
source_excerpt: Illustratively, some of the risks that the banks are generally exposed to but which are not captured or not fully captured in the regulatory CRAR would include: (a) Interest rate risk in the banking book; (b) Credit concentration risk; (c) Liquidity risk; (d) Settlement risk; (e) Reputational risk; (f) Strategic risk;

question: What does paragraph 12.10 require as a minimum from a bank's management as part of the ICAAP?
options: Periodic stress tests, particularly in respect of the bank's material risk exposures
A daily simulation of extreme movements in the securities market
Monthly stress tests covering every branch's cash position
A single stress test submitted along with the annual financial statements
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 12.10
source_excerpt: As part of the ICAAP, the management of a bank shall, as a minimum, conduct relevant stress tests periodically, particularly in respect of the bank's material risk exposures, in order to evaluate the potential vulnerability of the bank to some unlikely but plausible events or movements in the market conditions that could have an adverse impact on the bank.

question: Which statement matches Principle 3 of the Supervisory Review Process set out in paragraph 12.1.2?
options: Supervisors should expect banks to operate above the minimum regulatory capital ratios and should have the ability to require banks to hold capital in excess of the minimum
Banks should be permitted to operate exactly at the minimum regulatory capital ratios at all times
Supervisors should fix the interest rates that banks charge on their loans
Banks should be allowed to operate below the minimum regulatory capital ratios with prior permission
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 12.1.2
source_excerpt: Principle 3: Supervisors should expect banks to operate above the minimum regulatory capital ratios and should have the ability to require banks to hold capital in excess of the minimum.

question: Under paragraph 14.9.1, at what level of a banking group do Pillar 3 disclosures apply?
options: Only where a bank has foreign branches, with domestic subsidiaries left out
At the top consolidated level of the banking group to which the Capital Adequacy Framework applies
At the level of foreign branches of the bank only, with no requirement applying to the group as a whole
At the level of each listed associate of the bank separately, ignoring the group as a whole
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 14.9.1
source_excerpt: Pillar 3 applies at the top consolidated level of the banking group to which the Capital Adequacy Framework applies. Disclosures related to individual banks within the groups would not generally be required to be made by the parent bank.

question: According to paragraph 14.1.1, what is the aim of the market discipline disclosure requirements?
options: To allow market participants to assess information on scope of application, capital, risk exposures and risk assessment processes and hence the capital adequacy of the institution
To replace the supervisory review process conducted under Pillar 2
To publish the quarterly profit figures of the bank for its customers
To fix the minimum capital ratio that every bank must maintain
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 14.1.1
source_excerpt: The aim is to encourage market discipline by developing a set of disclosure requirements which will allow market participants to assess key pieces of information on the scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment processes and hence, the capital adequacy of the institution.

question: When is information regarded as material under the definition given in paragraph 14.5?
options: When its value exceeds a prescribed percentage of a bank's total assets
When accounting standards specifically require it to be published
When at least two market participants ask the bank for it
When its omission or misstatement could change or influence the assessment or decision of a user relying on that information for the purpose of making economic decisions
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 14.5
source_excerpt: Information would be regarded as material if its omission or misstatement could change or influence the assessment or decision of a user relying on that information for the purpose of making economic decisions.

question: How does paragraph 14.6 describe proprietary information?
options: Information about customers given to the bank under a legal agreement
Information that banks are exempt from disclosing under any circumstance
Information that becomes immaterial once it is more than a year old
Information that, if shared with competitors, would render a bank's investment in these products or systems less valuable and hence undermine its competitive position
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 14.6
source_excerpt: Proprietary information encompasses information (for example on products or systems), that if shared with competitors would render a bank's investment in these products/systems less valuable, and hence would undermine its competitive position.

question: According to paragraph 14.8, when did the Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures become effective and as on what date was the first set to be made?
options: Effective from July 1, 2013, with the first set as on September 30, 2013
Effective from September 30, 2013, with the first set of disclosures as on July 1, 2013
Effective from May 28, 2013, with the first set as on July 1, 2013
Effective from July 1, 2013, with the first set as on May 28, 2013
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 14.8
source_excerpt: Pillar 3 disclosures as introduced under Basel III have become effective from July 1, 2013. The first set of disclosures as required by these guidelines was to be made by banks as on September 30, 2013.

question: Under paragraph 14.9.2, how often must Pillar 3 disclosures generally be made, and how often for Tables DF-2, DF-3 and DF-4?
options: Quarterly for all disclosures, with no half yearly requirement
Half yearly for all disclosures, including Tables DF-2, DF-3 and DF-4 with no quarterly cycle
Annually for all disclosures, and quarterly for Tables DF-2, DF-3 and DF-4
At least half yearly generally, and at least quarterly for Tables DF-2, DF-3 and DF-4
source: Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, RBI/2025-26/08, DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Section 14.9.2
source_excerpt: Banks are required to make Pillar 3 disclosures 116 at least on a half yearly basis, irrespective of whether financial statements are audited, with the exception of following disclosures: (i) Table DF-2: Capital Adequacy; (ii) Table DF-3: Credit Risk: General Disclosures for All Banks; and (iii) Table DF-4: Credit Risk: Disclosures for Portfolios Subject to the Standardised Approach. The disclosures as indicated at (i), (ii) and (iii) above will be made at least on a quarterly basis by banks.

question: Under the Master Circular's definition in paragraph 2.1.1, when does an asset, including a leased asset, become non-performing?
options: When the account is not reviewed within 180 days of its due date
When it ceases to generate income for the bank
When the outstanding balance exceeds the sanctioned limit for 30 days
When the realisable value of security falls below 50 per cent
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 2.1.1
source_excerpt: An asset, including a leased asset, becomes non -performing when it ceases to generate income for the bank.

question: As per the list in paragraph 2.1.2, an instalment of principal or interest on a term loan must remain overdue for how long before the loan qualifies as a non-performing asset?
options: more than 30 days
more than 60 days
more than 120 days
more than 90 days
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 2.1.2
source_excerpt: interest and/ or instalment of princip al remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days in respect of a term loan

question: For short duration crops, after how many overdue crop seasons does an instalment of principal or interest make a loan a non-performing asset, as listed in paragraph 2.1.2?
options: one crop season
three crop seasons
two crop seasons
four crop seasons
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 2.1.2
source_excerpt: the instalment of principal or interest thereon remains overdue for two crop seasons for short duration crops

question: A CC/OD account's outstanding balance remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit. Under paragraph 2.2.1, for how long must this continue before the account is treated as out of order?
options: after 30 days
after 60 days
for 90 days
after 180 days
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 2.2.1
source_excerpt: The outstanding balance in the CC/OD account remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit/drawing power for 90 days

question: According to paragraph 2.3.1, when is any amount due to the bank under a credit facility regarded as overdue?
options: when it is not paid on the due date fixed by the bank
when it remains unpaid for more than 90 days
when the borrower's account has no credits for 90 days
when the bank fails to review the limit within six months
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 2.3.1
source_excerpt: Any amount due to the bank under any credit facility is ‘overdue’ if it is not paid on the due date fixed by the bank.

question: Under the income recognition policy stated in paragraph 3.1.1, how must a bank treat interest on an advance that is a non-performing asset?
options: Interest may be charged and taken to the income account on the due date
Interest may be taken to income account provided adequate margin is available
Banks should not charge and take to income account interest on any NPA
Interest may be recognised on accrual basis if the advance is Government guaranteed
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 3.1.1
source_excerpt: the banks should not charge and take to income account interest on any NPA. This will apply to Government guaranteed accounts also.

question: When an advance becomes a non-performing asset, what does paragraph 3.2.1 require banks to do with interest already accrued and credited to the income account in earlier periods?
options: Reverse only the interest relating to the last two quarters
Transfer the entire amount to a memorandum account without reversing it
Retain it because the advance carried a Government guarantee
Reverse the entire interest accrued and credited in the past periods if it is not realised
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 3.2.1
source_excerpt: If any advance, including bills purchased and discounted, becomes NPA, the entire interest accrued and credited to income account in the past periods, should be reversed if the same is not realised.

question: Under paragraph 3.3.1, interest realised on an NPA may be taken to the income account provided the credits towards interest do not arise from what source?
options: Repayment of the entire arrears of principal
Realisation of the security held against the advance
Fresh or additional credit facilities sanctioned to the borrower
Conversion of unpaid interest into a funded interest term loan
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 3.3.1
source_excerpt: Interest realised on NPAs may be taken  to income account provided the credits in the accounts towards interest are not out of fresh/ additional credit facilities sanctioned to the borrower concerned.

question: On an account turning NPA, paragraph 3.4 directs banks to reverse interest already charged but not collected. How is this done, and what may banks then do with the accrued interest?
options: By debiting a suspense account, after which the interest is written off permanently
By debiting the Profit and Loss account, after which accrued interest may be recorded in a Memorandum account
By crediting the capital reserve, after which no further record is kept
By debiting the borrower's account, after which interest continues to accrue on the advance
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 3.4
source_excerpt: On an account turning NPA, banks should reverse the interest already charged and not collected by debiting Profit and Loss account and stop further application of interest. However, banks may continue to record such accrued interest in a Memorandum account in their books.

question: According to paragraph 4.1.1, for how long must an asset have remained NPA for it to be classified as substandard?
options: less than 6 months
between 6 and 12 months
12 months or more
less than or equal to 12 months
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.1.1
source_excerpt: A substandard asset would be one, which has remained NPA for a period less than or equal to 12 months.

question: Under paragraph 4.1.2, an asset is classified as doubtful after it has remained in which category for a period of 12 months?
options: the standard category
the substandard category
the doubtful category
the loss category
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.1.2
source_excerpt: An asset would be classified as doubtful if it has remained in the substanda rd category for a period of 12 months.

question: Which of the following matches the definition of a loss asset given in paragraph 4.1.3 of the Master Circular?
options: An asset that has been written off wholly by the bank
An asset whose security value has eroded below 50 per cent of the assessed value
An asset where loss is identified but the amount has not been written off wholly
An asset that has remained in the doubtful category for more than three years
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.1.3
source_excerpt: A loss asset is one where loss has been identified by the bank or internal or external auditors or the RBI inspection , but the amount has not been written off wholly.

question: Regular and ad hoc credit limits must be reviewed or renewed not later than three months from the due date. According to paragraph 4.2.4, when is such an account treated as NPA if this is not done?
options: when the drawing power is calculated from a stock statement older than three months
if the limits have not been reviewed or renewed within 180 days from the due date
when the borrower's financial position is satisfactory despite irregular drawings
once the delay in review exceeds thirty days from the due date
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.4
source_excerpt: Hence, an account where the regular/ ad hoc credit limits have not been reviewed/ renewed within 180 days from the due date/ date of ad hoc sanction will be treated as NPA.

question: Under paragraph 4.2.4, when do irregular drawings in a working capital borrowal account make the account an NPA, even though the unit may be working or the borrower's financial position is satisfactory?
options: if they continue for a continuous period of 30 days
if they are permitted for a continuous period of 180 days
if the account's balance exceeds the sanctioned limit on the reporting date
if such irregular drawings are permitted in the account for a continuous period of 90 days
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.4
source_excerpt: A working capital borrowal account will become NPA if such irregular drawings are permitted in the account for a continuous period of 90 days even though the unit may be working or the borrower's financial position is satisfactory.

question: Under paragraph 4.2.5, when may a loan account classified as NPA be upgraded to the standard category?
options: only upon repayment of the entire arrears of interest and principal
once the account has remained regular for six consecutive quarters
when the realisable value of the security becomes adequate again
when the borrower pays one full instalment after the NPA classification
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.5
source_excerpt: In case of borrowers having more than one credit facility from a bank, loan accounts shall be upgraded from NPA to standard asset category only upon repayment of entire arrears of interest and principal pertaining to all the credit facilities.

question: Under paragraph 4.2.9.1, when is erosion in the value of security reckoned as significant, and how is such an NPA to be classified?
options: when realisable value falls below 25 per cent of the assessed value, classify as loss
when realisable value falls below 10 per cent of the outstanding, classify as doubtful
when realisable value is under 50 per cent of the assessed value, classify as doubtful
when realisable value is less than 50 per cent of the outstanding, classify as substandard
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.9
source_excerpt: Erosion in the value of security can be reckoned as significant when the realisable value of the security is less than 50 per cent of the value assessed by the bank or accepted by RBI at the time of last i nspection, as the case may be. Such NPAs may be straightaway classified under doubtful category.

question: If the realisable value of the security, as assessed by the bank, approved valuers or RBI, is less than 10 per cent of the outstanding in the borrowal account, what does paragraph 4.2.9.1 direct the bank to do?
options: ignore the existence of the security and classify the asset straightaway as loss asset
classify the asset straightaway as doubtful and provide 100 per cent of the unsecured portion
make an additional provision of 10 per cent over the substandard provision
classify the asset as substandard and review its classification after one year
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.9
source_excerpt: If the realisable value of the security, as assessed by the bank/ approved valuers/ RBI is less than 10 per cent of the outstanding in the borrowal accounts, the existence of security should be ignored and the asset should be straightaway classified as loss asset.

question: Banks should normally provide for the entire amount due immediately upon a fraud being detected. What smoothing option does paragraph 4.2.9.2 permit for this provisioning?
options: spreading the provision over a period not exceeding eight quarters
making the provisions over a period not exceeding four quarters of detection
debiting only the profit and loss account in the first quarter and reversing the provision later
providing 50 per cent at once and the balance after the next RBI inspection
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.9
source_excerpt: However, to smoothen the effect of such provisioning on quarterly profit and loss, banks have the option to make the provisions over a period, not exceeding four quarters, commencing from the quarter in which the fraud has been detected

question: According to paragraph 4.2.14.1, when may a credit facility backed by the guarantee of the Central Government be treated as an NPA even though it is overdue?
options: when interest on the facility remains overdue for more than 90 days
only when the Government repudiates its guarantee when invoked
when the borrower fails to make payment for two consecutive quarters
when the guarantee is invoked and the amount remains unpaid for six months
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.14
source_excerpt: The credit facilities backed by guarantee of the Central  Government though overdue may be treated as NPA only when the Government repudiates its guarantee when invoked.

question: Under paragraph 4.2.19.2, when is a credit card account treated as a non-performing asset?
options: when the total billed amount is not paid within 30 days of the due date
when the account remains past due for more than three days
when only the minimum amount due is paid for three consecutive monthly billing statements
when the minimum amount due is not paid fully within 90 days from the payment due date
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 4.2.19
source_excerpt: A credit card account will be treated as non -performing asset if the minimum amount due, as mentioned in the statement, is not paid fully within 90 days from the payment due date mentioned in the statement.

question: Loss assets should be written off. If loss assets are permitted to remain in the books for any reason, what does paragraph 5.2 of the Master Circular require?
options: 15 per cent of the outstanding should be provided for
25 per cent of the outstanding should be provided for
50 per cent of the outstanding should be provided for
100 per cent of the outstanding should be provided for
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 5.2
source_excerpt: Loss assets should be written off. If loss assets are permitted to remain in the books for any reason, 100 percent of the outstanding should be provided for.

question: An advance has remained in the doubtful category for two years. As per the provisioning table in paragraph 5.3.2, what rate applies to the secured portion of such an advance?
options: 25 per cent
30 per cent
40 per cent
100 per cent
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, Table at paragraph 5.3.2
source_excerpt: Period for which the advance has remained in ‘doubtful’ category Provisioning requirement (%) Up to one year 25 One to three years 40 More than three years 100

question: What general provision does paragraph 5.4.1 of the Master Circular require on the total outstanding of a substandard asset, without any allowance for ECGC cover or securities?
options: 10 per cent
15 per cent
20 per cent
25 per cent
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 5.4.1
source_excerpt: A general provision of 15 percent on total outstanding should be made without making any allowance for ECGC guarantee cover and securities available.

question: Infrastructure loan accounts classified as substandard, where banks have an escrow mechanism for cash flows and a clear legal first claim on them, attract what provisioning under paragraph 5.4.2?
options: 20 per cent instead of the aforesaid prescription of 25 per cent
10 per cent instead of the aforesaid prescription of 15 per cent
25 per cent instead of the aforesaid prescription of 40 per cent
15 per cent instead of the aforesaid prescription of 20 per cent
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 5.4.2
source_excerpt: However, in view of certain safeguards such as escrow accounts available in respect of infrastructure lending, infrastructure loan accounts which are classified as sub-standard will attract a provisioning of 20 per cent instead of the aforesaid prescription of 25 per cent. To avail of this benefit of lower provisioning, the banks should have in place an appropriate mechanism to escrow the cash flows and also have a clear and legal first claim on these cash flows.

question: Which of the following categories attracts a standard asset provision of 0.25 per cent under paragraph 5.5.1 of the Master Circular?
options: Farm Credit to agricultural activities, individual housing loans and Small and Micro Enterprises (SMEs)
Advances to the Commercial Real Estate sector
Advances to the Commercial Real Estate - Residential Housing sector
All other loans and advances not included in the listed categories
source: Master Circular - Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances, RBI/2025-26/13, DOR.STR.REC.9/21.04.048/2025-26, April 01, 2025, Part A, paragraph 5.5.1
source_excerpt: Farm Credit to agricultural activities , individual housing loans and Small and Micro Enterprises (SMEs) sectors at 0.25 per cent;
